scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The origin of Thacholikali is traced back to ancient days in the Malabar region when Kalarippayattu was in vogue.
It is classified as a form of 'actual' Kolkali, a traditional folk art that evolved by drawing elements from martial training.
Unlike the more contemporary Thekkan Koladi, Thacholikali maintains a direct link to the historical combat techniques of Kerala.
on_screen: Map: India · South Asia

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Thacholikali was traditionally performed during festivals and communal gatherings.
It serves as a display of rhythmic precision and physical agility.
Currently, it is recognized as a rare art form that is at risk of disappearing, representing a specific historical layer of Kerala's folk traditions.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers move in a circle, striking small sticks to keep rhythm.
The choreography involves the circle expanding and contracting as the dance progresses.
The footwork and body postures are taken directly from Kalarippayattu, requiring significant physical conditioning.
Watch for Stick striking, Circle contraction.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The primary sound is produced by the striking of small wooden sticks held by the dancers.
This is accompanied by vocal music that follows a specific rhythmic structure.
Listen for the Small wooden sticks.

The sound is dominated by the sharp, percussive clacking of wooden sticks struck in unison. This is layered over vocal chanting or singing that starts at a lower register and steadily climbs in volume and pitch as the dance intensifies.
